newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 to focus on currency rates, growth.
newsitem.headline: G7 to focus on currency rates, growth.

text.p: Senior officials of the Group of Seven nations Monday put worries about currency rates and economic growth on the agenda for a meeting of the world's top finance officials in Berlin this weekend.
Details of the meeting of deputy finance ministers, which was held in Germany's financial capital of Frankfurt, were not released and officials had no comment on the discussions.

But a German government source said the talks had focused on the state of the world economy and exchange rate developments, as well as international development aid and the need for closer cooperation between supervisory authorities.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in an interview with Sunday's Berliner Morgenpost that these issues, together with Europe's plans to create a single currency, would be the focus of Sunday's meeting.
"The issues in our Berlin meeting will be the global economic conditions for growth, world trade, and of course exchange rates," Waigel told the newspaper.

He added, "Our colleagues from North America and Japan are very interested in receiving reports on the developments in Europe at first hand," he said. "That is why I have put the euro on the agenda for the meeting."
For financial markets, however, the immediate focus of the meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors is likely to lie in any comments on the dollar.

Markets are looking keenly for any hints that the Group of Seven -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- were unhappy with a roaring 6.5 percent rise in the dollar against the mark last month.

Although the G7 itself talked the U.S. currency higher after it plunged to all-time lows in 1995, some fear that the recent surge may have come a little too fast to appease concerns that markets are becoming disorderly.
German central bank President Hans Tietmeyer and other Bundesbank officials sent a clear signal to markets last week that the dollar's rise could not go on at this pace.
U.S. industry is also starting to feel the bite of the currency increase on its export trade.
